title: Multicomponent synergistic immobilization via in-situ and dynamic exchange strategies for constructing hierarchical biopharmaceuticals

paper_content.abstract: Hierarchical immobilization of multicomponent biomacromolecules has been demonstrated to be a favorable protocol for constructing advanced biopharmaceuticals, but still with formidable challenges. Herein, we innovate a multicomponent synergistic immobilization approach combining an in-situ method with a structural-transformation-promoted dynamic exchange method in a flexible zeolitic pyrimidine framework (ZPF) platform to construct multicomponent biopharmaceuticals. In-depth mechanism investigation reveals that special functional groups (e.g., carboxyl, sulfhydryl, imidazolyl) on protein surface can significantly promote the dynamic structural transformation of ZPF and allow for the efficient immobilization of proteins on the surface of ZPF crystals via dynamic exchange approach. By combining with the in-situ method, which can immobilize biomacromolecules in the inner part of ZPF crystals, multicomponent biomacromolecules can be regionally localized within ZPF crystals. This controlled spatial preparation provides substantial advantages over conventional core-shell architectures for cascading enzyme immobilization and enables the development of advanced anticancer agents demonstrating enhanced therapeutic efficacy for female Balb/c nu mice. Moreover, this platform can also generate highly efficient hierarchical antibacterial formulations to significantly enhance the wound-healing process of male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats. This study provides a revolution to immobilize multicomponent biomacromolecules and represents an innovative and effective platform of biopharmaceuticals with immense potential for anticancer and antibacterial formulations.
paper_content.introduction:
Biological macromolecules, including proteins, nucleic acids, and polysaccharides, are essential and fundamental large molecules that play critical roles in sustaining life, regulating organismal functions, and facilitating the transmission of genetic information. Investigating the synergistic use of biomacromolecules is of great significance for accumulating scientific theories and technological advances in a wider range of fundamental sciences. However, the utilization of such biomacromolecules faces several challenges. For instance, packaging multiple biomacromolecules into one system with a rational design to achieve a synergistic effect remains challenging due to the intrinsically varied characteristics of each molecule. Furthermore, after encapsulation, maintaining stability and biocompatibility of the whole system under various conditions, such as varied temperature, pH, and ionic strength, also requires considerable effort, particularly for in vivo applications.

The applications of these multicomponent biomacromolecules are diverse, including enzyme immobilization and the development of biopharmaceuticals, such as therapeutic agents targeting cancer or bacterial infections. To ensure effective immobilization and delivery, carriers that provide protection, stabilization, and controlled release of the biomacromolecules are often employed. However, conventional immobilization strategies face challenges, including biomacromolecule inactivation, poor carrier stability, and limited versatility. Particularly, the immobilized enzyme carrier often causes the enzyme activity to decrease, and the ordered enzyme distribution inside the carrier is often challenging to achieve. Furthermore, it is difficult to adjust the position of different components in their carriers. To address these issues, it is urgently essential to develop carriers and immobilization methods that can facilitate the positioning, proportion, and quantification of multicomponent biomacromolecules to achieve a synergistic effect.

Over the past two decades, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as one of the most attractive functional supramolecular materials due to their adaptable and defined structures, high porosity, tunable pore size, and customizable functionality. MOFs have demonstrated great potential in diverse research fields, including gas adsorption and separation, chemical sensing, heterogeneous catalysis, and especially the immobilization of biomacromolecules for biopharmaceuticals. The immobilization methods of MOFs for biomacromolecules mainly include pore adsorption, covalent grafting, and in-situ encapsulation. Among them, the in-situ immobilization method, which simulates the phase separation of natural biological macromolecules, offers the significant advantage of being capable of immobilizing biological molecules regardless of their size. However, previously reported MOFs capable of enzyme immobilization under ambient aqueous conditions remain exceedingly rare (<10). Furthermore, conventional methodologies (e.g., core-shell methods) suffer mass transfer barriers and lack precise control over biomolecular spatial distribution within these materials, which presents significant challenges, particularly for multicomponent enzyme systems. Recently, our group has developed a dynamic exchange strategy (also named dynamic defect generation strategy) for enzyme immobilization, utilizing the dissociation equilibrium of MOFs mediated by enzymes. This approach enables the uniform loading of enzymes onto the material surface, circumventing the size limitations of biomacromolecules. Thus, combining the in-situ and dynamic exchange strategies in one system can achieve the regional distribution of multicomponent biomacromolecules and facilitate their immobilization and function, but this has not yet been realized.

In this study, aiming to address the challenges associated with the spatial immobilization of multicomponent biomacromolecules, we have developed a multicomponent synergistic approach integrating in-situ and dynamic exchange methods to construct multicomponent biopharmaceutical formulations within a flexible MOF structure synthesized under ambient aqueous conditions—ZPF-8 (ZPF = zeolitic pyrimidine framework). The resulting bio-composites could realize a hierarchical localization of multicomponent proteins, hence serving as highly efficient anticancer or wound-healing biopharmaceuticals. The discovery and utilization of ZPF-8 advance the design and synthesis of versatile platforms for combining multicomponent biomacromolecules and establish the guiding principles for developing biopharmaceutical platforms.
paper_content.results:
Immobilization of biomacromolecules by the in-situ method
Pyrimidine plays a crucial role in biological systems, not only as an essential base in nucleic acids but also as a participant in metabolic processes and genetic information transmission. Furthermore, it exhibits significant potential for applications in the pharmaceutical domain. Our group has reported a flexible zinc-based zeolitic pyrimidine framework (ZPF-2), which can be synthesized at room temperature in an aqueous solution, hence benefiting the immobilization of enzymes via an in-situ method. That is, enzymes can be immobilized during the formation process of ZPF-2 crystals. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) characterization suggested that the actual crystal structure of ZPF-2 fitted with the theoretical simulation. Notably, this is the inaugural instance where the structure of ZPF-2-Zn can be precisely determined by using single-crystal data. The results of Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA), Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images, N2 and CO2 adsorption-desorption of the synthesized ZPF-2 were also found to be consistent with the literature. To explore the ability of ZPF-2 to immobilize enzymes, we then used ZPF-2 to immobilize enzymes (e.g., glucose oxidase (GOx)) via an in-situ assembly approach (GOx@ZPF-2, @=in-situ immobilization). GOx@ZPF-2 retained the initial PXRD pattern and SEM morphology of ZPF-2, while Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) spectra showed the characteristic peaks of GOx in GOx@ZPF-2. To investigate the distribution of GOx, ZPF-2 was synthesized in FITC-tagged GOx solution, and a Super-Resolution Imaging System (SIM) was conducted. The SIM images demonstrated that FITC-labeled GOx was uniformly distributed inside the GOx@ZPF-2.

Immobilization of biomacromolecules by the dynamic exchange method
Subsequently, we further explored whether ZPF-2 could undergo the traditional dynamic exchange approach to achieve surface immobilization of enzymes, which could further construct a multi-enzyme regional distribution system. However, when ZPF-2 was immersed directly into the solution of GOx, we found that it barely immobilized the enzyme, indicating that ZPF-2 was challenging to be triggered by the enzyme molecules to dissociate and create defects for enzyme immobilization. Interestingly, we discovered that after treating ZPF-2 with acetone, THF, DMSO, 1,4-dioxane, or ethyl acetate, PXRD results revealed that ZPF-2 could transform into a phase (named ZPF-8) exhibiting a distinct PXRD pattern. SCXRD characterization suggested ZPF-8 has nearly the same coordinate environment as ZPF-2 but crystallizes in higher symmetry, i.e., the cubic I-43m space group (a=b=c=15.8963 Å, α=β=γ=90°, V=4016.9 Å3). The topological structure and coordination environment of ZPF-8 are almost identical to those of the well-known ZIF-8. A face-to-face comparison of the structures of ZPF-2 and ZPF-8 found differences between the coordinates of the coordinate bonds and dihedral angles of ligands with 6-membered rings. These results indicate that upon stimulation with specific solvents, the F-pym ligand can rotate, thus leading to structural transformation. It should be noted that it belongs to a single-crystal-to-single-crystal transformation process, not the typical dissolve-regenerate pathway.

The transition process from ZPF-2 to ZPF-8 was then investigated in an in situ fashion. PXRD patterns of the transition states showed the gradual disappearance of the ZPF-2 peaks and the appearance of ZPF-8. Quantitative analysis of each transition state showed the deceleration of these transformations until all ZPF-2 microsized crystals transformed to ZPF-8. Interestingly, by simply immersing ZPF-8 in the water for a certain time (e.g., 24 h), ZPF-8 could transform back to ZPF-2. Both processes could be performed repeatedly upon altering the solvents for five cycles. These interesting structure transformation processes were then investigated in depth via FT-IR spectra. After immersing ZPF-8 in water, the characteristic peaks of Zn–H2O (γ(Zn–O) at 495 cm−1 and ρ (H2O) at 557 cm−1) appeared initially and then disappeared gradually. This phenomena proved that the Zn–N bonds in ZPF-8 could be partially dissociated upon the attack of water molecules. Then, they reformed after extending the immersion time, forming a more stable structure in the water environment, i.e., ZPF-2. TGA traces and SEM images for ZPF-8 showed similar results with ZPF-2, while its CO2 adsorption-desorption isotherm showed a typical type I isotherm and adsorbed ~40 cm3/g of CO2 at ~100 kPa, indicative of a more rigid structure. Besides, the transformed ZPF-2 from ZPF-8 showed a feature very similar to that of pristine ZPF-2, suggesting complete reversibility of the structural transformation.

The dynamic nature and mild structural transformation conditions of ZPF-8 encouraged us to try the immobilization of biomacromolecules. ZPF-8 was immersed in an aqueous solution of GOx as a demonstration. A time-dependent loading curve was displayed, and the loading amount increased gradually with the extension of the loading time and approached a saturation of 0.12 g/g after 20 min. The PXRD pattern of the formed product (named as GOx⊂ZPF-2, ⊂=dynamic exchange immobilization) confirmed the successful transition from ZPF-8 to ZPF-2. FT-IR also showed the characteristic peaks of GOx in GOx⊂ZPF-2. To further investigate the distribution of GOx, ZPF-8 was soaked in FITC-tagged GOx solution for different times. The SIM images demonstrated that FITC-labeled GOx was mainly embedded in the outer layer of ZPF-2 particles, and the thickness of GOx entry increased with increasing loading time.

Accordingly, one can reason that the disintegration and reorganization process of the framework would be the driving force facilitating the encapsulation of GOx during the structural transformation from ZPF-8 to ZPF-2. To further explore the mechanism of enzyme encapsulation during immobilization, we also monitored the changes in soaking solutions via 1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H NMR). After the same soaking time in GOx solution, the ligand signal of ZPF-8 rose significantly (nearly two times compared with pure D2O), while pristine ZPF-2 released almost no ligands into D2O. This phenomenon indicated the generation of more defects on MOFs and the coordinate bonds mediated by GOx, which should come from the interaction between functional groups on proteins with metal ions. To prove this, 19 natural amino acids (except Tyr, which had a low solubility) were screened to identify which functional groups (-R) could promote this process via different immobilization efficiencies of ZPF-8. The results showed that the significantly high loading capacities of Cys (0.14 g/g), Glu (0.035 g/g), Asp (0.083 g/g), and His (0.10 g/g) suggested that besides predicted carboxyl, sulfhydryl and imidazolyl in proteins could also possibly promote the enzyme immobilization. To further prove this conclusion, seven glycine-based dipeptides and four polypeptides with different sizes were also tested, suggesting that the immobilization efficiencies had a positive correlation with the ratio of Cys+Glu+Asp+His in these peptides total amino acids. These comparisons proved that after “activating” ZPF-2 into ZPF-8 and then immersing it in enzyme solution, proteins could generate more competitive coordination against original ligands during the dynamic structural transformation and enzyme immobilization process. Finally, along with original ligand release and defect generation, the coordination and immobilization of enzymes within the MOF structures were achieved.

To study the effect of soaking time on the catalytic performance of the encapsulated enzyme, we investigated the relationship between enzyme activity and loading time. The activity increased gradually with the extension of the loading time and approached its highest at ~20 min. Notably, GOx⊂ZPF-2 could fully retain the free enzyme activity. Theoretically, immobilized enzymes on the surface of particles would greatly promote catalytic performance because they could expose more active enzymes from the material surface. To highlight the advantages of this dynamic structural transformation approach, we also used GOx@ZPF-2 as a comparison. It was found that the encapsulated enzymes retained 90% of their activity (loading amount: 0.15 g/g). All these findings further demonstrate that the dynamic transformation induces the formation of more defects in the material, resulting in a higher enzyme loading compared to the conventional defect generation strategy (0.12 vs 0.04 g/g), which exhibits meaningless enzymatic activity due to insufficient loading capacity. Compared with free GOx, GOx⊂ZPF-2 retained over half of its initial activity under various harsh conditions (e.g., GOx⊂ZPF-2 exposure to 70 °C, remaining activity = ~100%, trypsin: 56%; while free GOx only retained <15% under the same treating conditions). Furthermore, GOx⊂ZPF-2 could maintain approximately 80% of its catalytic activity after 10 recycles and retain its crystallinity and morphology. However, only 25% of the remaining activity of GOx@ZPF-2 was observed. It is possible because enzymes encapsulated inside the crystal catalyze the substrate, and then the produced H2O2 accumulates and partially damages the carrier from the inside. These results indicated that enzyme⊂ZPF-2 is an excellent enzyme immobilization platform with superior biocatalytic performance and superior cyclic catalytic capacity.

In practical applications, multi-enzyme systems are often required to achieve advanced catalytic functions, presenting significant challenges for rational construction and optimization. For example, GOx can catalyze the oxidation of glucose to gluconic acid while simultaneously generating hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which subsequently serves as a substrate for catalase (CAT). Co-immobilization of these two enzymes could effectively verify the feasibility of enzyme cascade reactions. To systematically explore the influence of spatial distribution on cascade reaction efficiency, we developed a synergistic immobilization strategy. Initially, GOx was incorporated into the ZPF-2 via an in-situ synthesis method (i.e., GOx@ZPF-2), followed by selective immobilization of CAT onto these composite structures through a dynamic exchange method (during the transformation from GOx@ZPF-2 to GOx@ZPF-8, the enzymatic activity of GOx was fully retained), thereby establishing a GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 cascade system. This synergistic strategy exploits the complementary characteristics of both immobilization methods: the in-situ embedded GOx remains stably anchored within the crystal core through multiple coordination interactions established during framework assembly, while the subsequent dynamic exchange process—triggered by the ZPF-8→ZPF-2 transformation—generates surface defects and coordination vacancies that selectively capture CAT at the particle surface. This spatially programmed architecture creates an optimal substrate channeling pathway where glucose diffuses inward to react with core-embedded GOx, and the generated H2O2 is immediately consumed by the surface-localized CAT, minimizing intermediate accumulation and preventing oxidative damage to both enzymes and the framework structure. The hierarchical localization was confirmed by SIM images. The catalytic performance of this hierarchical design was rigorously compared with two approaches: (I) a traditional core-shell configuration (GOx@ZPF-2@CAT@ZPF-2) and (II) simultaneous co-immobilization of both enzymes via dynamic exchange (GOx&CAT⊂ZPF-2). Under standardized conditions, maintaining equivalent enzyme loading capacities and ratios (GOx:CAT = 1:1) across all configurations, the GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 system exhibited superior catalytic efficiency, achieving >200% relative activity compared to the alternative materials. These results convincingly demonstrate the critical importance of optimizing both the regional cascade distribution of enzymes and simultaneously maximizing enzyme-substrate interactions for enhanced catalytic performance. The recyclability of the optimized GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 system was evaluated through ten consecutive catalytic cycles. The system maintained approximately 80% of its initial activity, demonstrating substantial operational stability attributed to the rapid consumption of the generated H2O2 intermediate via CAT.

The hierarchical immobilization strategy demonstrated above extends beyond enzymatic cascade catalysis to encompass diverse multicomponent biomedical systems requiring precise spatio-temporal coordination. In advanced therapeutic applications, distinct biomolecular components must function in orchestrated sequences—targeting moieties and therapeutic proteins in tumor therapy must operate sequentially to achieve site-specific accumulation followed by localized drug action, while in wound healing applications, antimicrobial agents and tissue repair factors necessitate programmed release profiles to combat infection before promoting regeneration. These complex biomedical scenarios uniformly demand spatially compartmentalized delivery systems that can regulate the sequential presentation of multiple bioactive components, thereby maximizing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing off-target effects.

Construction of multicomponent anti-tumor biopharmaceuticals
The starvation therapy for cancer, as an approach to treating malignant tumors, could consume the glucose reserves of tumor cells to eliminate cancer cells. We then tried to combine in-situ and dynamic exchange methods to construct multicomponent synergistic formulations. For example, transferrin (Tf), known for its strong selective binding to the abundant transferrin receptors on the surface of tumor cells, can be utilized for targeted drug delivery to tumor cells. By employing Tf in a carrier, GOx can be directly transported into cancer cells, inducing apoptosis through intracellular glucose consumption. So we incorporated GOx into ZPF-2, then immobilized Tf onto these composite structures, forming GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 multicomponent synergistic system. The hierarchical localization was confirmed by utilizing FITC-labeled GOx and RhB-labeled Tf, which was conducted via SIM images. The pH-responsive property of GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 revealed remarkable stability at physiological pH (7.4) — exhibiting merely 15% GOx release after 5 h. Conversely, under acidic conditions (cancer cell’s lysosomal environment), material rapidly released GOx (a notable 90% at pH 4.6, 5 h) — indicating the carrier’s response capability to environmental stimuli and promoting the bioactive interaction between GOx and glucose within the tumor microenvironment.

The cytotoxicity of GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 was evaluated in vitro via MTT assay. This study involved two representative cancer cell lines (HeLa and MCF-7) and a normal cell line (3T3) to assess the cytotoxicity. Compared to the control ZPF-2, which exhibited half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 58.05 μg/mL, the viability of HeLa cells notably decreased when treated with GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 (IC50 = 39.77 μg/mL). This suggests that the encapsulation of GOx and Tf within the nanoparticles enhanced the toxicity against the cancer cells. Conversely, negligible cytotoxicity was observed in 3T3 cells within the nanoparticle concentration range of 0–40 μg/mL. The study also explored other counterpart multicomponent synergistic systems created through a similar method. Remarkably, adjusting the protein configuration within the nanoparticles could increase the values of IC50. These results confirm that the enhanced cytotoxic effect is primarily due to the specific hierarchical distribution of the anti-tumor multicomponent synergistic system. To further support these findings, FITC-labeled materials were analyzed to assess cellular uptake capabilities through a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM). The images revealed a pronounced increase in green fluorescence in cells, indicating that surface-incorporated Tf significantly enhances cellular uptake by effectively targeting transferrin receptors, thereby leading to a marked accumulation of the material in HeLa cells.

The rational design of nanoparticle components and their ratios is crucial for optimizing cancer therapy. By immobilizing both proteins within the ZPF-2 structure, we could also adjust the GOx/Tf ratio to optimize anti-tumor efficiency. The optimized GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 nanoparticles (GOx:Tf = 1.1:1) yielded the lowest IC50 values of 39.77 μg/mL and 68.00 μg/mL for HeLa and MCF-7 cells, respectively. Additionally, we tested the universality of this approach by integrating two different anticancer agents—5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and apoptin caspase 3—into similar systems. The assembled composites demonstrated significant anti-tumor activity, surpassing their counterparts without Tf. Furthermore, we combined cancer-starving therapy with small-molecule drugs to enhance the killing effect of the combined formulation on tumor cells, via incorporating 5-FU into GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 to assess its anti-tumor properties. Synthesized GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 nanoparticles exhibited remarkable cytotoxicity at lower concentrations against both HeLa and MCF-7 cells (IC50 = 25.38 or 54.01 μg/mL), confirming a significant enhancement in the combined anti-tumor effects via the design and regulation of this hierarchical multicomponent synergistic system.

After assessing the anti-tumor effect in vitro, the multicomponent synergistic tumor inhibition effect of GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 was evaluated using a subcutaneous HeLa tumor-bearing female Balb/c nu mouse model. Throughout the therapeutic period (11 days), negligible fluctuations in mice’s body weights were observed following various treatments. Digital photographs and spider plots visually confirmed that the tumors in the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 group were nearly eliminated, and the corresponding tumor-bearing ratio had decreased significantly, verifying the prominent multicomponent synergistic therapeutic outcome. The relative tumor volume curves for different groups are presented, and the corresponding tumor growth inhibition (TGI) rates were calculated, while the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 group was found to be the highest (73.26%). In contrast, other control groups showed negligible tumor suppression or continued growth, comprehensively demonstrating the synergistic efficacy of our strategy. To investigate the therapeutic mechanism, an H&E staining assay was performed to investigate the histological damage and apoptosis levels in the tumors. As shown, severe morphological changes and apoptosis were observed in the tumors of GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 group. In contrast, no significant damage were detected in the tumors treated with the counterpart groups, further validating the synergistic effects mediated by the multicomponent system. These results clearly demonstrate the excellent therapeutic outcome exerted by GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2, which can be attributed to several factors. Primarily, Tf is utilized for targeted drug delivery to tumor cells. Subsequently, GOx mediates the competitive consumption of tumorous glucose while, simultaneously, 5-FU directly kills cancer cells. In summary, GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2, as a multicomponent synergistic anti-tumor system, potently inhibits tumor growth through hierarchical localization.

Construction of multicomponent anti-bacteria biopharmaceuticals for wound healing
Skin, the largest sensory organ, serves as a protective barrier for the human body against external damage. Wounds on the skin frequently develop in various situations, and the blood or blood clot in the early phases of hemostasis provides a nourishing culture media for the growth of invading bacteria. The above promising multicomponent synergistic anti-tumor results have also inspired the further construction of multicomponent synergistic anti-bacteria formulations to form composite agents for application in wound healing. By adjusting the distribution of the components within the system, it is possible to target the various phases of wound healing. Extraordinary, nisin, known for its strong inhibitory effect on many gram-positive bacteria, can be utilized in the initial inflammation phase to eliminate invading bacteria. Zn2+ in MOFs can promote the proliferation of fibroblasts and collagen synthesis, which is conducive to the growth of granulation tissue. Additionally, trypsin (Tps) can provide powerful support for the maturation phase by eliminating inflammatory secretions, breaking down denatured proteins, and promoting tissue regeneration. Considering the above positive factors, Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 multicomponent synergistic system could be formed for wound healing. The hierarchical localization was confirmed by SIM images. The in vitro antibacterial activity of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 was evaluated using minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) standard tests against Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC 29213). Under the same nisin concentration (MIC of free nisin = 50 mg/L), the antibacterial effects of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 were found to be very close to free nisin, while an insignificant antibacterial effect was observed for ZPF-2. The results demonstrated that our reversible deformation strategy did not affect the antimicrobial properties of the encapsulated nisin. These preliminary results showed the feasibility of applying this synergistic immobilization strategy to build antibacterial formulations through hierarchical localization for wound healing.

To further evaluate the wound healing capacity of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 in vivo, experiments were conducted on the dorsum of male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats. Results showed the wound contraction for Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 was superior to other groups, exhibiting the best wound healing capacity even on the 3rd day. The percentages of wound area closure at different healing times were calculated, revealing that after 7th days, wounds treated with Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 achieved significant closure of ~95%, compared to the control, which showed ~75% wound closure. Remarkably, after 14th day of treatment with Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2, the wounds healed completely, with 100% wound contraction, demonstrating a highly improved wound healing ability. These results indicate that multicomponent synergistic anti-bacteria systems can be beneficial and effective for accelerating wound healing, due to the multicomponent synergies in Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2.

Histopathological studies were carried out to further compare the wound healing efficiencies via hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) and Masson’s staining. After 7th day, wounded tissues in the control group still exhibited numerous immune cell infiltrations. Surprisingly, for Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2, inflammatory cell infiltration was suppressed, and a significantly higher number of fibroblasts was observed around the impaired region. After 14th day, compared to the irregular structure in control, the wounds treated with Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 showed higher density and volume fraction of collagen, greater regularity of both epithelium and connective tissue with more fibroblasts, a complete epithelium structure, and regenerated hair follicles and blood vessels. Tissue of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2 group exhibited excellent wound healing characteristics, facilitating a faster and more effective re-epithelization process, connective tissue remodeling and arrangement, and the formation of a more regular structure with increased hair follicle formation. This can be attributed to the excellent multicomponent synergistic properties of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2, promoting overall wound healing.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated the construction of a dynamic zeolitic pyrimidine framework to enable precise and efficient regulation of multicomponent combinations of biomacromolecules. This flexible MOF possesses the ability to either immobilize biomacromolecules via an in-situ method or via a structural-transformation-promoted dynamic exchange method. The structural transformation process and enzyme immobilization mechanism were unveiled in-depth via various characterizations, including SCXRD, in situ PXRD, FT-IR, etc. We found that the Zn-N bonds in the ZPF structure could be partially dissociated, then reversibly reformed upon the attack of water molecules, accompanied by ligand movement, rotation, and recombination. This structural transformation allows for the immobilization of enzymes on the outer part of the framework, which is challenging to achieve by the traditional immobilization strategies. Our findings suggest that proteins can produce more competitive coordination from their sulfhydryl, carboxyl, and imidazolyl functional groups, ultimately promoting enzyme immobilization. The resulting biocatalysts exhibited superior biocatalytic performance, protective capabilities, and superior cyclic catalytic capacity. Notably, by combining the in-situ method with the dynamic exchange method in one system, various multicomponent biomacromolecule formulations with hierarchical localization can be constructed, such as cascading enzyme immobilization, anti-tumor and anti-bacteria multicomponent formulations. For instance, cascading immobilized enzyme preparations demonstrated a two-fold enhancement in catalytic activity compared to conventional core-shell structured formulations. Furthermore, a multicomponent biopharmaceutical with co-immobilization of transferrin, GOx and 5-FU led to enhanced therapeutic performance, confirmed by in vitro and in vivo anti-tumor experiments. Further, by incorporating the antibacterial nisin and the wound healing-promoting trypsin, advanced antibacterial formulations for wound healing were successfully constructed through hierarchical localization, while simultaneously utilizing the components of the ZPF to significantly enhance the wound healing process through in vitro and in vivo experiments. This study enriches the toolbox for biomacromolecule immobilization and provides a synergistic approach for fabricating multicomponent biopharmaceuticals.
paper_content.methods:
General
Except for the special description, chemicals like Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (Innochem, AR), 5-fluoro-2-hydroxypyrimidine (Innochem, 97%), 5-FU (Innochem, 99%), Nisin (Innochem, 98%), organic solvents (Innochem, AR), and biological reagents like GOx (Solarbio, 10 KU), CAT (Solarbio, BR), transferrin (Solarbio, 98%), trypsin (Solarbio, BR) throughout the experiments, were purchased from commercial sources and used as received without further purification. All cell lines certification is provided by the ATCC company from which they originated. Animal experiments on anti-tumor were approved by the Animal Research Committee of Nankai University, China (Approval Number: 2023-SYDWLL-000641), and were carried out strictly according to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Research Council, 1996). Animals used in wound healing experiments complied with the National Research Council’s Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and these procedures were reviewed and approved by the Committee for the Care and Use of Animals at the Tianjin University of Science & Technology in China (Approval Number: SYXK2023-0003).

Characterization
SCXRD data were collected at 120 K via an Oxford Cryostream system on a SuperNova (Mo) X-ray Source with a micro-focus sealed X-ray tube. The structure was solved and refined using Olex2 with ‘XS’ and ‘XL’ plug-in. Hitachi UH-5300 UV-vis spectrophotometer was used to record the catalytic process. The absorbance value was measured with the SpectraMax M2e microplate reader. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of all materials were collected at ambient temperature with a Rigaku dmax 2500 diffractometer operated at 40 kV and 40 mA using Cu Kα (λ=1.5418 Å) radiation, with a scan speed of 1 sec/step, a step size of 0.02° in 2θ, and a 2θ range of 5° to 40°. Crude data were subjected to baseline correction and analyzed by Jade 6. The low-pressure CO2 adsorption and desorption isotherms were measured at 195 K using a Micromeritics ASAP 2460 instrument. Before gas adsorption measurements, the samples were outgassed at 95 °C for 24 h before the measurements. Fourier transform infrared spectrophotometer (FT-IR) spectra of all materials were obtained using a Thermo Fisher spectrometer with ATR modes. The confocal images experiments were performed on a Zeiss Elyra 7 Super-Resolution Imaging System (SIM) with a 63× objective oil lens. The Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) images were recorded on Leica TCS SP8.

Synthesis of ZPF-8
Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (1 mmol) was dissolved in deionized water (5 mL), and 5-fluoro-2-hydroxypyrimidine (2 mmol dissolved in 5 mL of water) was added under stirring. The clear solutions were kept at room temperature for about 5 min, and then the pH was raised to 4.5 by adding 1M base (NaOH, KOH, or NH3·H2O). The precipitate was harvested by centrifugation at 4000xg for 1 min and then washed twice with deionized water to obtain ZPF-2. As-synthesized ZPF-2 powder was immersed in THF for 24 h to obtain ZPF-8.

Synthesis of GOx⊂ZPFs
GOx solution (3 mg/mL) was prepared by dissolving GOx in 50 mM MES buffer (pH=6.0). 15 mg as-synthesized ZPF-8 was ultrasonically dispersed in 1 mL GOx solution, and incubated in a 37 °C shaker for 1, 2, 4, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 60 min, respectively. The solid was collected by centrifuge and washed with DI water twice. The supernatants were collected to determine the amount of immobilized GOx in MOFs. The uptake amount was determined by the Bradford method. The loading efficiency (LE%) and loading capacity (LC, g/g) were calculated as follows:
LE% = (total protein - protein in supernatant) / total protein × 100% (1)
LC = protein loaded into materials / weight of materials (2)

Catalytic performance of GOx, and GOx⊂ZPFs composites
The activity of GOx was determined through the 3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) method, which is used to detect the concentration of glucose. 100 μg GOx (or GOx⊂ZPFs composites containing 100 μg GOx) were added into 0.91 mL aqueous solution. After that, 90 μL of glucose solution (50 mM) was added. After 7 min, 30 μL of the supernatant was taken and mixed with 60 μL DNS solution. The mixture was heated at 100 °C for 5 min. Hitachi UH-5300 UV-vis spectrophotometer was used to record the catalytic process. After cooling to room temperature, the final glucose concentrations were monitored by measuring the absorbance at 540 nm and compared with the standard curve to calculate the final glucose concentration.

Synthesis of GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2
3 mg GOx was added to the aqueous solutions of 5-fluoro-2-hydroxypyrimidine (0.2 M, 667 μL). Zinc nitrate hexahydrate was dissolved in deionized water (0.2 M, 333 μL). These two aqueous solutions were mixed and placed at room temperature for 20 min. The solid was collected by centrifugation and washed with DI water and DMSO twice, respectively. As-synthesized GOx@ZPF-2 powder was immersed in DMSO and incubated at room temperature on a shaker for 20 min to obtain GOx@ZPF-8, then collected by centrifugation. Transferrin solution (3 mg/mL) was prepared by dissolving transferrin in 50 mM HEPES buffer (pH=7.0). As-synthesized GOx@ZPF-8 was ultrasonically dispersed in 1 mL transferrin solution, and incubated at room temperature on a shaker for 20 min to obtain GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2. The solid was collected by centrifugation and washed with DI water twice. The supernatants were collected to determine the amount of immobilized GOx or transferrin in MOFs. The uptake amount was determined by the Bradford method.

In vivo anticancer therapeutic evaluation
Tumor (HeLa) bearing Balb/c nu mice (female, 6 weeks of age) were randomly divided into 4 groups (n=5). When the tumor volume reached about 100 mm3, the mice were intratumorally injected with Normal saline (100 µL), 5-FU (156 μg/mL, 100 μL), GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2, GOx&5-FU@ZPF-2, and GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 (the corresponding 5-FU was 156 μg/mL, 100 μL), respectively. Prior to the initiation of the experiment, the rats were anesthetized with isoflurane (3% to 4% for induction and 2% to 2.5% throughout the surgical procedure) to ensure the maintenance of a stable state. The tumor volume and body weight of mice were recorded every other day. The tumor volume was calculated as follows: V = W2 × L/2, where W and L represented the tumor width and length, respectively. The mice were sacrificed 11 days post-treatment, and the tumors were collected and photographed. The tumor growth inhibition (TGI) rate was calculated according to the equation.
TGI = (1 - VT / VC) × 100% (3)
Where VC represents the tumor volume of the control group, and VT represents the tumor volume after the treatments.
Simultaneously, the tumors of the mice were collected and used for histological and H&E staining assay, and the tumor size of all experimental animals did not exceed 20 mm as stated in the ethical review documents.

Wound healing assay
A full-layer skin defect infection model was used to evaluate the wound healing of Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (male, 180–200 g, 6–8 weeks of age), and 25 rats were randomly divided into 5 groups. Prior to the initiation of the experiment, the rats were anesthetized with isoflurane (3% to 4% for induction and 2% to 2.5% throughout the surgical procedure) to ensure the maintenance of a stable state. After anesthesia, shave the back and disinfect it with medical alcohol. A circular full-layer excision wound (8 mm diameter) was produced with a biopsy perforator (Japan, BP-80F). Each wound was inoculated with 50 μL Staphylococcus aureus suspension (OD600=0.3). Leave the bacterial suspension on the wound for 30 min. They were treated with PBS (Control), nisin, ZPF-2, Nisin⊂ZPF-2, and Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2, respectively. After that, the wound area was immobilized with sterile gauze. Wound photos were taken on days 0, 3, 7, 10 and 14, and the wound size was quantified by Image J software. The healing process takes about 14 days. Freshly regenerated skin tissue was collected on days 7 and 14. These tissues were immobilized in 4% PFA solution for 48 h. Wound healing was evaluated by H&E and Masson staining. Sex was considered in the study design, and detailed information was described in the manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, Chen’s group elucidate a cascade immobilization methodology that synergistically integrates in-situ
immobilization processes with dynamic exchange immobilization techniques for the fabrication of hierarchically-structured
multicomponent biopharmaceutical systems. The investigation employs zeolitic pyrimidine frameworks as versatile and
reversible matrices, facilitating the immobilization of biomacromolecules with precise spatial orientation and distribution.
This strategic approach demonstrates significant implications for the advancement of complex biopharmaceutical
formulations where spatial control of bioactive components is important for therapeutic efficacy and functional performance.
Thus, I highly recommend it be accepted after a minor revision.
Comments 1: Obviously, this cascade immobilization approach shows higher advantages over the core-shell method. The
comparison should be emphasized in the introduction part.
Comments 2: A comparative analysis of the enzymatic activities between GOx⊂ZPF-2 and materials from conventional
defect generation strategy should be incorporated into the manuscript. In the event that materials from conventional defect
generation strategy exhibit meaningless enzymatic activity due to insufficient loading capacity, authors should add the
corresponding description in the corresponding part.
Comments 3: For recyclability of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2, the authors should clarify what the initial activity is.
Comments 4: During the enzyme immobilization, the pH of the enzyme solution should also be considered as to whether it
affects the structural transformation and defect generation of the MOFs
Comments 5: Some figures are too small, e.g., Supplementary Figure 47. The authors should make some adjustments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The current manuscript presents a strategy for achieving reversible encapsulation of enzymes and proteins by exploiting the
dynamic conformational response of ZPF-2 to various solvents, including acetone, THF, DMSO, 1,4-dioxane, and ethyl
acetate. By combining an in-situ encapsulation approach for inner-layer enzymes with a dynamic exchange method for
outer-layer enzymes, the authors developed several systems: a hierarchical cascade enzyme system (GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2),
multi-component anti-tumor agents (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2), and antibacterial formulations (Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2). Among these,
only the first qualifies as a cascade system, whereas the latter two consist of independently functioning proteins that do not
engage in interdependent interactions. The manuscript has several critical shortcomings. Most notably, it fails to clearly
demonstrate the innovation, necessity, and uniqueness of the proposed reversible encapsulation strategy when compared
with existing methods (Nature Catalysis, 2018, 1(9): 689–695; Angew. Chem.
Int. Ed., 2023, 62, e202302436). The preparation of GOx@ZPF-2 via an in-situ method followed by organic solvent-induced outer-layer enzyme replacement
does not appear to offer substantial advantages over established techniques. The current data do not provide convincing
evidence to demonstrate the spatial distribution of the different components within the hierarchical cascade enzyme system.
The manuscript also suffers from a lack of narrative coherence. The first half focuses on a cascade enzyme system
(GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2), while the second half abruptly transition to multi-component systems (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 and
Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2) that are not cascade-related, in which the relevance of these systems to the initial design rationale
remains unclear. Moreover, the necessity of employing the complex reversible encapsulation strategy in the latter systems is
not sufficiently justified, further weakening the overall conceptual continuity. In conclusion, I do not recommend this
manuscript for publication in its current form. While it explores the use of ZPF-2 for
encapsulating cascade enzymes and multicomponent protein systems, it does
not convincingly demonstrate the benefits or uniqueness of the proposed
dynamic encapsulation strategy. Instead, it adds unnecessary complexity and
leaves key design rationales insufficiently justified. A transfer to a more
specialized journal may be more appropriate.
Other important issues should also be considered and addressed:
(1) While the authors point out the limited spatial control in traditional enzyme loading strategies using MOFs—such as in
situ encapsulation and covalent attachment—the nanoparticles prepared in this study exhibit significant heterogeneity in
both size and morphology. This raises concerns about whether the proposed approach truly offers improved precision in
enzyme distribution and loading as claimed.
(2) During the construction of the GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 system, GOx@ZPF-2 undergoes a conformational transformation into
GOx@ZPF-8 upon exposure to organic solvents such as acetone, THF, DMSO, 1,4-dioxane, or ethyl acetate. It is unclear
whether this solvent treatment affects the catalytic activity of GOx. Given the known sensitivity of enzymes to external
environment, this warrants further clarification and possibly experimental validation.
(3) For the cascade enzyme system (GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2), as well as the multi-component anti-tumor agent (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-
2) and antimicrobial agent (Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2), what is the loading capacity of each enzyme per nanoparticle? How was
this determined, and was the quantification accurately performed using fluorescence quantification methods? Considering
that the fluorescent molecules are not covalently linked to the enzyme molecules, questions arise regarding the precision
and reliability of this approach. Was this fluorescence quantification cross-validated against thermogravimetric analysis
(TGA) or other independent methods? The quantification process should be thoroughly detailed, including the specific
protocols and controls used.
(4) Some data analysis lacks depth and is insufficient to fully support the conclusions; for instance, FTIR characterization did
not reveal significant differences, and the relationship between enzyme fluorescence quantification data and
thermogravimetric data was not thoroughly investigated. In Figure S7, both samples (GOx@ZPF-2 and ZPF-2) show
essentially identical peaks with only minor shifts. This similarity undermines the claim that GOx is exclusively present in one
sample. Likewise, the interpretations based on FTIR spectra (Figures S21, S30b, and S31b) are not sufficiently supported by
the data and may not be accurate.
(5) For the cascade enzyme system (GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2), as well as the multi-component anti-tumor agent (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-
2) and the antimicrobial agent (Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2), apart from SIM images of GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 in Fig 3c, there is no direct
evidence provided regarding the spatial distribution of other enzymes. The authors are advised to provide more visually
intuitive characterization results to substantiate their claims of controlled enzyme localization.
(6) The manuscript highlights limitations of conventional immobilization strategies, including difficulties in achieving ordered
enzyme distribution and precise spatial control. However, prior studies, particularly those involving MOFs and DNA origami
have demonstrated the feasibility of spatially organized, multi-enzyme assemblies. In this context, the manuscript does not
convincingly demonstrate how the proposed strategy offers a clear advantage over these existing approaches, especially in
terms of spatial accuracy, individual enzyme activity, or cascade reaction efficiency.
(7) In the stability comparison shown in Figure S30, the enzyme activities of free GOx (5%), GOx⊂ZPF-2 (55%), and
GOx@ZPF (79%) were reported. While the GOx⊂ZPF-2 system immobilizes GOx on the outer surface of ZPF crystals using
a dynamic exchange method, a notably higher reduction in GOx activity was observed under trypsin treatment. This
observation contradicts the authors’ claim regarding the superior stability of this system.
(8) I understand that GOx@ZPF-2 could exhibit improved environmental stability compared to free GOx. However, the
GOx⊂ZPF-2 system, prepared via dynamic exchange and thus not tightly encapsulated within the MOF framework, still
retains most of its initial activity under various harsh conditions, which is somewhat unexpected and deserves further
clarification.
(9) The reported enhancement of the MOF-confined biocascade system is intriguing. However, considering the relatively
small aperture size of ZPF-2, it is expected that substrate and intermediate diffusion would be restricted, especially given the
spatially separated enzyme arrangement. This apparent improvement in catalytic performance requires further explanation.
(10) In comparing bioactivity across different materials, how to ensure the loadings of each enzyme or protein were
consistent among different groups, particularly in co-encapsulation system. the manuscript does not clarify how this
consistency was achieved, and the reported enzyme/protein loadings appear to vary across different materials, which may
confound the interpretation of bioactivity differences.
(11) For the multi-component anti-tumor agent (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2) and the antimicrobial agent (Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2), the term
"cascading" is not accurate; it would be more appropriate to describe their mechanism as a "multi-component synergistic
effect".
(12) This strategy does not provide clear advantages over cancer treatment methods involving cascade enzymes,
photothermal therapy, and drug targeting. Since the manuscript discusses the preparation of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2, why not
utilize GOx@CAT⊂Tf⊂ZPF-2 for cancer therapy?
(13) For GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 with an average particle size of 150 nm based on DLS measurements (Figure S37),
particularly TEM images reveal significant particle size heterogeneity. Considering this, can the Super-Resolution Imaging
System (SIM) reliably distinguish between GOx and Tf?
(14) Many cascade catalytic systems have been reported previously. The authors should cite relevant studies and provide a
quantitative comparison of their results with the existing literature. Such a comparison is essential to justify the necessity and
advantages of the hierarchical spatial arrangement strategy proposed in this work.
(15) In evaluating the anti-tumor effects, digital images (Figure 4b) demonstrate that the tumors in the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-
2 group were almost entirely eradicated, with a significant reduction in tumor burden, which validates the therapeutic effect.
To provide a more comprehensive illustration of the treatment process, the authors are advised to include digital images
showing the tumor growth suppression over time (e.g., on days 3, 5, and 7). Moreover, the mice in v (11 d) appear
excessively large with swollen abdomens, raising concerns about whether this is a normal observation. How does the
synergistic tumor suppression efficacy of the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 system compare with that of other anti-tumor
strategies?
(16) How should one interpret the sentence "However, previously reported MOFs which were capable of being synthesized
under ambient aqueous conditions while simultaneously facilitating enzyme encapsulation remains exceedingly limited
(<10)32." in the manuscript (on page 4 line 79)?
(17) Can the dynamic behavior be leveraged to control the amount of enzyme or protein encapsulated within and outside the
nanoparticles, particularly by modulating the inner-to-outer diameter ratio? How is the loading capacity related to kinetic
behavior? Does the influence of different solvents on the dynamic properties differ?
(18) The references to the SI figures in lines 123–131 are incorrectly numbered. The authors should carefully verify and
correct all SI figure citations to ensure accuracy and clarity.

Distinction from ZIF-8 systems (Nature Catalysis, 2018): While conventional
one-pot co-immobilization strategies successfully achieve multi-enzyme
encapsulation, they fundamentally cannot address the critical challenge of
spatial distribution of multi-enzymes. CLSM analysis in the literature
confirms uniform enzyme distribution throughout the framework. Subsequent
studies have required multi-step synthetic approaches to generate core-
shell architectures for achieving spatial distribution (Nat. Commun. 2022, 13,
305; Small 2025, 21, 2503059), thereby demonstrating the necessity of
spatial distribution for enhanced cascade efficiency. In contrast, our
approach exploits ZPFs' unique solvent-responsive properties to achieve, for
the first time, hierarchical immobilization through in-situ encapsulation (inner-
layer enzymes) and dynamic exchange (outer-layer enzymes) under ambient
conditions while preserving MOF structural integrity.
Distinction from UiO-66 systems (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2023): The dynamic
defect generation strategy is limited to zirconium-based MOFs such as UiO-
66. Moreover, the ball-milling method for in-situ enzyme immobilization is
severely restricted to mechanically robust enzymes (e.g., lipase, GOx) and
limited MOFs such as UiO-66 and ZIF-8. Thus, developing new platforms to
construct hierarchical multicomponent biocatalysts or
biopharmaceuticals is of great importance. Our ZPF-2-based dynamic
conformational strategy integrates the advantages of both approaches while
extending applicability to virtually any protein cargo, significantly
broadening the scope of immobilization strategies and enabling applications in
advanced pharmaceutical formulations.

demonstrate spatial distribution. By differentially labeling inner-layer enzymes

Figure 3c. SIM images of GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2.

Figure S1. SIM images of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2.
Figure S2. SIM images of Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2.

innovation of our manuscript is the development of a versatile MOF-based
immobilization platforms that enable the spatial distribution of diverse
biomolecules. To demonstrate the broad applicability of this strategy, we
systematically explored its implementation in various contexts, including
enzymatic cascade catalysis and synergistic therapeutic formulations for
cancer treatment and wound healing.

MOF systems. Compared to ZIF-8 systems, conventional one-pot strategies
achieve multi-enzyme encapsulation but fail to provide spatial distribution.
Regarding UiO-66 systems, dynamic defect generation strategy are limited to
zirconium-based MOFs and applicable only to mechanically robust enzymes,
severely restricting their utility. Our strategy combines advantages of both
approaches while offering spatial accuracy and universal applicability to diverse
protein cargoes.
While DNA origami offers partially spatial control, several intrinsic limitations
constrain their practical application. First, the synthesis of DNA scaffolds and
subsequent enzyme conjugation requires sophisticated molecular biology
techniques, resulting in substantial economic and technical barriers. More
critically, enzymes tethered to DNA scaffolds through conventional
bioconjugation strategies retain significant conformational flexibility due to the
inherent flexibility of enzymes. This molecular mobility, fundamentally
compromises the precision of spatial control and long-term stability of the
enzyme assembly. Furthermore, DNA-based systems exhibit limited chemical
stability under physiological conditions and are susceptible to nuclease
degradation, restricting their applicability in complex biological environments.
(Nanomaterials 2016, 6, 139; Appl. Microbiol. Biotechnol. 2023, 107, 9.).
Regarding individual enzyme activity, our data demonstrate that GOx⊂ZPF-2
retains 100% activity while GOx@ZPF-2 maintains 90% activity. Critically, the
GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 cascade system exhibits over 100% activity enhancement
compared to both core-shell (GOx@ZPF-2@CAT@ZPF-2) and co-immobilized
via dynamic exchange (GOx&CAT⊂ZPF-2) controls, substantiating superior
cascade reaction efficiency through spatial distribution (Figure S35).
Figure S11. Comparison of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 with GOx@ZPF-
2@CAT@ZPF-2 and GOx&CAT⊂ZPF-2 for the conversion of glucose
oxidation.
(7) In the stability comparison shown in Figure S30, the enzyme activities of
free GOx (5%), GOx⊂ZPF-2 (55%), and GOx@ZPF (79%) were reported.
While the GOx⊂ZPF-2 system immobilizes GOx on the outer surface of ZPF
crystals using a dynamic exchange method, a notably higher reduction in GOx
activity was observed under trypsin treatment. This observation contradicts the
authors’ claim regarding the superior stability of this system.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. While GOx⊂ZPF-2
retains 55% activity under trypsin treatment compared to 79% for GOx@ZPF-
2, it represents an 10-fold improvement over free GOx (5% retention),
demonstrating substantial protective effects. Per the suggestion of the reviewer,
we revised our description to more accurately state as "Compared with free
GOx, GOx⊂ZPF-2 retained over half of its initial activity under various harsh
conditions" in page 11, paragraph 1.
(8) I understand that GOx@ZPF-2 could exhibit improved environmental
stability compared to free GOx. However, the GOx⊂ZPF-2 system, prepared
via dynamic exchange and thus not tightly encapsulated within the MOF
framework, still retains most of its initial activity under various harsh conditions,
which is somewhat unexpected and deserves further clarification.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. As documented in the
literature (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2023, 62, e202302436) and our manuscript,
“Enzymes can act as “macro ligands” to generate competitive coordination
against original ligands, along with the release of metal of MOFs to generate
defects, hence promoting the immobilization of enzymes”, and “proteins can
produce more competitive coordination from their sulfhydryl, carboxyl, and
imidazolyl functional groups, ultimately promoting enzyme immobilization.”
I.e., proteins function as "macro-ligands" that generate competitive coordination
with MOF metal centers, inducing defect formation. Subsequently, proteins are
not merely embedded within defects but establish multiple coordination
interactions through sulfhydryl, carboxyl, and imidazolyl functional groups with
exposed metal sites. This multivalent binding creates a robust enzyme-MOF
interface, significantly enhancing stability beyond simple physical entrapment.
(9) The reported enhancement of the MOF-confined biocascade system is
intriguing. However, considering the relatively small aperture size of ZPF-2,
it is expected that substrate and intermediate diffusion would be restricted,
especially given the spatially separated enzyme arrangement. This apparent
improvement in catalytic performance requires further explanation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. ZPF shares identical
topology (sod) with ZIF-8, exhibiting similar pore dimensions (~0.35 nm), which
exceed glucose molecular size (~0.30 nm). As demonstrated in the cited Nature
Catalysis, 2018, 1(9): 689–695, ZIF-8 successfully facilitates glucose cascade
oxidation with encapsulated GOx and HRP, confirming substrate accessibility
through framework pores. Moreover, the ZIF-8 multi-enzyme cascade system
with a core-shell structure also confirmed that spatial distribution of enzyme can
also improve the catalytic effect (Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 305). Our observed
performance enhancement in the ZPF-2 system, utilizing CAT instead of HRP,
is therefore consistent with established precedent while benefiting from our
spatial distribution strategy.
(10) In comparing bioactivity across different materials, how to ensure the
loadings of each enzyme or protein were consistent among different groups,
particularly in co-encapsulation system. the manuscript does not clarify how this
consistency was achieved, and the reported enzyme/protein loadings appear to vary across different materials, which may
confound the interpretation of bioactivity differences.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. Our protocol ensures
uniformity through batch preparation: Initial in-situ protein loading is performed
on a large batch of ZPF-2 materials, which is subsequently divided into equal
aliquots for structural transformation and secondary protein loading. Protein
solutions for secondary loading are likewise prepared from a single stock and
dispensed in equal volumes. This approach minimizes inter-sample variability
within experimental series. Furthermore, all characterization and evaluation
experiments will be conducted simultaneously using materials from the same
synthesis batch containing the same quality of drugs (e.g., GOx@ZPFs
composites containing 100 μg GOx), ensuring rigorous comparability across
experimental groups. Per the suggestion of the reviewer, we included this
preparation protocols in the Supporting Information to ensure reproducibility.
(11) For the multi-component anti-tumor agent (GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2) and the
antimicrobial agent (Tps@Nisin⊂ZPF-2), the term "cascading" is not accurate;
it would be more appropriate to describe their mechanism as a "multi-
component synergistic effect".
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. Per the suggestion of the
reviewer, we consistently described all systems as exhibiting "multi-component
synergistic effect," emphasizing how spatiotemporal coordination enhances
catalytic or therapeutic outcomes.
(12) This strategy does not provide clear advantages over cancer treatment
methods involving cascade enzymes, photothermal therapy, and drug targeting.
Since the manuscript discusses the preparation of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2, why not
utilize GOx@CAT⊂Tf⊂ZPF-2 for cancer therapy?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. It is important to clarify
that our spatial distribution strategy represents a platform technology that
complements, rather than competes with, existing therapeutic modalities such
as cascade enzymes, photothermal therapy, and drug targeting. These
established anticancer strategies typically employ multi-component
formulations that could theoretically benefit from spatial distribution (INT J BIOL
MACROMOL, 2025, 306, 141581.; INT J BIOL MACROMOL, 2024, 278,
134746.; Neoplasia, 2024, 56, 101024.). Our methodology provides a versatile
framework for reconstructing these formulations with enhanced spatial control,
potentially improving their therapeutic efficacy through optimized component
distribution and sequential release profiles. We envision future applications
where our platform technology could be integrated with these various
therapeutic approaches to create next-generation combination therapies.
Regarding GOx@CAT@Tf⊂ZPF-2, our preliminary investigations have indeed
demonstrated its feasibility and enhanced anticancer efficacy. However, for this
manuscript, we strategically selected the combination of small-molecule drugs
with macromolecular therapeutics to comprehensively demonstrate the
versatility of our loading strategy across diverse molecular architectures. This
deliberate choice establishes the versatility of our platform, providing a
foundation for future investigations that may incorporate cascade enzyme
systems, photothermal agents, drug targeting, or other advanced therapeutic
modalities.
(13) For GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 with an average particle size of 150 nm based on
DLS measurements (Figure S37), particularly TEM images reveal significant
particle size heterogeneity. Considering this, can the Super-Resolution Imaging
System (SIM) reliably distinguish between GOx and Tf?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. The SIM typically
achieves resolution of approximately 50 nm, while our SEM characterization
indicates particle sizes ranging from 50-500 nm, providing adequate resolution
for accurate discrimination. Furthermore, to enhance observational reliability,
we employed differential fluorescent labeling with FITC-GOx (green
fluorescence) and RhB-Tf (red fluorescence), and selected particles with a size
close to 200 nm for observation. The distinct spectral separation between these
fluorophores ensures unambiguous differentiation and accurate spatial
localization data.
(14) Many cascade catalytic systems have been reported previously. The
authors should cite relevant studies and provide a quantitative comparison of
their results with the existing literature. Such a comparison is essential to justify
the necessity and advantages of the hierarchical spatial arrangement strategy
proposed in this work.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. In our study, we
specifically employed core-shell (GOx@ZPF-2@CAT@ZPF-2) and co-
immobilization via dynamic exchange (GOx&CAT⊂ZPF-2) systems as internal
controls, demonstrating 100% activity enhancement in our hierarchical system,
substantiating superior cascade reaction efficiency (Figure S35).
Figure S12. Comparison of GOx@CAT⊂ZPF-2 with GOx@ZPF-
2@CAT@ZPF-2 and GOx&CAT⊂ZPF-2 for the conversion of glucose
oxidation.
Per the suggestion of the reviewer, we expanded our literature comparison to
include additional relevant studies (e.g., Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 305; Small
2025, 21, 2503059) to strengthen the comparative analysis and highlight the
advantages of our spatial organization strategy.
(15) In evaluating the anti-tumor effects, digital images (Figure 4b) demonstrate
that the tumors in the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 group were almost entirely
eradicated, with a significant reduction in tumor burden, which validates the
therapeutic effect. To provide a more comprehensive illustration of the
treatment process, the authors are advised to include digital images showing
the tumor growth suppression over time (e.g., on days 3, 5, and 7). Moreover,
the mice in v (11 d) appear excessively large with swollen abdomens, raising
concerns about whether this is a normal observation. How does the
synergistic tumor suppression efficacy of the GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 system compare with
that of other anti-tumor strategies?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. We appreciate the
reviewer's suggestion regarding the inclusion of time-course digital images to
comprehensively illustrate the tumor growth suppression dynamics. We fully
recognize the scientific value of visual documentation in demonstrating
temporal changes during therapeutic intervention. In accordance with our
experimental protocol, we conducted systematic tumor volume measurements
at predefined intervals (days 0, 3, 6, 9, and 11) throughout the treatment period.
Photographic documentation was acquired at the initial time point (day 0) and
terminal endpoint (day 11) to capture the overall therapeutic outcome.
Regarding the supplementation of intermediate time-point imaging (days 3, 6,
and 9), we would like to respectfully highlight the current discourse in the
oncological literature concerning optimal data presentation methodologies.
While certain studies have employed sequential photographic documentation
to capture morphological changes, substantial evidences indicate that
quantitative tumor growth kinetics, presented as continuous curves, provide
more robust and statistically rigorous assessment of therapeutic efficacy (e.g.,
Adv. Healthc. Mater., 2022, 11, 2102298.; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 2954.; Nat.
Commun., 2024, 15, 8695.; Adv. Healthc. Mater., 2024, 13, 2303911.; ACS
nano, 2022, 16, 20975-20984.; Adv. Mater., 2021, 33, 2100333.; ACS Appl.
Mater. Interfaces, 2024, 16, 12289-12301.). This approach minimizes potential
observational bias associated with single-time-point imaging and ensures
reproducibility of results. To comprehensively address the reviewer's
suggestion while maintaining methodological rigor, we have incorporated a new
Figure S47 in the revised manuscript, presenting the data as a spider plot—a
visualization method widely adopted in oncological literature. This
multidimensional representation integrates temporal dynamics with individual
tumor growth trajectories, enabling simultaneous assessment of both individual
response heterogeneity and population-level therapeutic trends. This analytical
approach preserves the granularity of individual data points while facilitating
statistical interpretation of treatment efficacy across the entire experimental
cohort.
Figure S13. Spider plots of individual tumor growth curves.
Regarding the appearance of mice in group v (day 11), the apparent abdominal
distension may be attributed to photographic angle and handling position. Per
the suggestion of the reviewer, we selected another representative image to
ensure accurate visual documentation.
Figure 4c. Photos of tumor dissection.
The GOx&5-FU@Tf⊂ZPF-2 system, integrating small-molecule drugs,
macromolecular therapeutics, and targeting proteins in spatially segregated
domains, achieved a tumor growth inhibition (TGI) rate of 73.26%. In contrast,
control groups (I: control; II: 5-FU; III: GOx@Tf⊂ZPF-2 without small-molecule
loading; IV: GOx&5-FU@ZPF-2 without targeting protein loading) showed
negligible tumor suppression or continued growth, comprehensively
demonstrating the synergistic efficacy of our strategy. Per the suggestion of the
reviewer, we incorporated these contents into the main text as “In contrast,
other control groups showed negligible tumor suppression or continued growth,
comprehensively demonstrating the synergistic efficacy of our strategy” in page
16, paragraph 2.
(16) How should one interpret the sentence "However, previously reported
MOFs which were capable of being synthesized under ambient aqueous
conditions while simultaneously facilitating enzyme encapsulation remains
exceedingly limited (<10)32." in the manuscript (on page 4 line 79)?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. We apologize for the
ambiguous phrasing. The intended meaning is among reported literature,
MOFs capable of enzyme immobilization under ambient aqueous conditions
remain exceedingly rare (<10). Per the suggestion of the reviewer, we revised
this sentence as “However, previously reported MOFs capable of enzyme
immobilization under ambient aqueous conditions remain exceedingly rare
(<10)” in page 3, paragraph 1, to enhance clarity and readability.
(17) Can the dynamic behavior be leveraged to control the amount of enzyme
or protein encapsulated within and outside the nanoparticles, particularly by
modulating the inner-to-outer diameter ratio? How is the loading capacity
related to kinetic behavior? Does the influence of different solvents on the
dynamic properties differ?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. The progressive
enhancement of fluorescence intensity from outer-layer enzymes, as
documented in Figures S22 and 2a, provides compelling evidence for time-
dependent loading augmentation and spatial distribution expansion.
Figure S22, 2a. SIM images of A FITC-GOx⊂ZPF-2 (1 min), B FITC-
GOx⊂ZPF-2 (10 min), and C FITC-GOx⊂ZPF-2 (20 min).
This observation is also corroborated by Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2023, 62,
e202302436, which employed SIM to visualize similar loading dynamics (Figure
R1).
Figure R1. SIM images of FITC-lipase@UiO-66 for different immobilization
times.
These observations confirm that the ZPF system exhibits dynamic protein-
framework interactions that can be leveraged to modulate both the quantity and
spatial distribution of proteins within the outer layer. The time-dependent nature
of this process provides a controllable parameter for tuning protein loading
density and distribution volume. Complementarily, conventional in-situ
encapsulation methods offer precise control over enzyme loading through
adjustment of initial enzyme concentrations during synthesis (Chem. Rev. 2021,
121, 1077.; ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 13, 56752.). This established
approach provides direct regulation of the enzyme quantity within the inner core
region. By strategically combining these two approaches, we can effectively
modulate both the enzyme loading and the spatial distribution between inner
and outer regions, i.e., enable systematic control over the inner-to-outer
diameter ratio.
Our kinetic analysis (Figure 2a) reveals that enzyme loading follows a
characteristic saturation profile, with loading capacity increasing gradually over
time and approaching an equilibrium value of 0.12 g/g after 20 minutes. This
further proves from another perspective that the timing of controlling dynamic
behaviors can regulate the amount of enzyme or protein encapsulated within
and outside the nanoparticles.

Regarding solvent-dependent transformation kinetics, we acknowledge that
different solvents possess distinct physicochemical properties (e.g., molecular
size, lipophilicity, dielectric constant) that theoretically influence structural
transformation rates. To ensure complete and reproducible transformations, we

Figure S9. PXRD patterns of soaked in different solvents.

The authors should carefully verify and correct all SI figure citations to ensure

significance and rigor of our study. We remain committed to improving our
